subject: surgery
title: Surgical Site Infections, Cellulitis, and Necrotising Fasciitis

steps.tx: Infections occurring at the operative incision within thirty days of a surgical procedure are classified as a **surgical site infection**. If an artificial prosthetic implant remains in situ, the monitoring window extends to ninety days. Accounting for twenty percent of all healthcare-associated infections, surgical site infections increase postoperative morbidity, prolong hospital stay, and elevate healthcare costs. The primary microbial culprit across most surgical specialties remains Staphylococcus aureus.
steps.say: Infections developing at the surgical incision within thirty days are classified as surgical site infections. They represent one fifth of all hospital infections, with Staphylococcus aureus remaining the leading pathogen.

rows: Any anatomical cavity opened or manipulated

steps.tx: Superficial dermal infections that spread diffusely through subcutaneous tissue without suppurative collections represent **cellulitis**. Typically triggered by beta-haemolytic streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus entering through small cutaneous breaks, cellulitis presents with poorly demarcated, spreading erythema, localized heat, oedema, and marked tenderness. Linear erythematous streaks extending toward regional lymph nodes indicate ascending lymphangitis, signaling the need for prompt intravenous antibiotic therapy targeting Gram-positive cocci.
steps.say: Cellulitis is a non-suppurative infection spreading diffusely through subcutaneous layers. Patients exhibit spreading erythema, warmth, and pain, requiring prompt intravenous antibiotics targeting streptococci and staphylococci.

steps.tx: When local tissue necrosis leads to a focal, walled-off accumulation of purulent exudate, the lesion is termed an **abscess**. Clinically, an abscess is characterized by warmth, rubor, throbbing pain, and the cardinal sign of fluctuance elicited by alternating bimanual palpation. Because the surrounding fibrous pseudocapsule prevents systemic antibiotics from penetrating into the avascular purulent cavity, systemic antibiotic monotherapy is ineffective without definitive source control.
steps.say: An abscess is a localized, walled-off accumulation of pus exhibiting fluctuance on palpation. Because the thick pseudocapsule blocks antibiotic penetration, physical drainage is mandatory for cure.

right.title: Cutaneous Abscess
points: Surrounded by an indurated inflammatory wall
Requires mandatory surgical incision and drainage

steps.tx: The definitive treatment of any fluctuant abscess is prompt **incision and drainage**, classically executed utilizing the Hilton method. An incision is made along relaxed skin tension lines over the point of maximal fluctuance. Closed sinus forceps are introduced into the cavity and opened widely in multiple directions to break down all internal loculations, followed by thorough saline irrigation and loose ribbon gauze packing.
steps.say: Definitive management requires incision and drainage via the Hilton method. Surgeons make an incision along tension lines and insert sinus forceps to disrupt loculations and evacuate all pus.

vis.alt: Incision and drainage of an abscess using the Hilton method.
vis.caption: Incision and drainage of an abscess demonstrating loculation breakdown. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial destruction of subcutaneous tissue and superficial fascia is known as **necrotising fasciitis**. The disease spreads along avascular fascial planes with alarming speed while initially sparing overlying skin and deeper muscle. Patients display severe systemic toxicity, marked tachycardia, and the pathognomonic clinical feature of extreme pain out of proportion to the mild overlying cutaneous erythema.
steps.say: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency involving rapid destruction of subcutaneous fascia. Patients exhibit profound toxicity and severe pain that is strikingly out of proportion to early skin findings.

nodes.label: Minor puncture, surgical cut, or perianal crypt infection
Rapid bacterial proliferation along avascular superficial fascia
Microvascular thrombosis of perforating nutrient skin vessels
Skin bullae, sensory anaesthesia, and patchy cutaneous gangrene

steps.tx: Microbiologically, necrotising soft tissue infections are stratified into two primary distinct classes. **Type I necrotising fasciitis** is polymicrobial, representing synergistic co-infection by mixed aerobes and anaerobes such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Bacteroides, and Peptostreptococcus, characteristically occurring in elderly diabetics. In contrast, Type II is monomicrobial, caused by virulent Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, occurring even in young, healthy hosts.
steps.say: Necrotising infections are stratified microbiologically. Type one is polymicrobial, mixing aerobes and anaerobes in diabetic hosts, whereas type two is monomicrobial, driven by group A streptococci.

left.title: Type I (Polymicrobial)
points: Predominates in diabetics and obese patients
Often produces subcutaneous gas on radiography

right.title: Type II (Monomicrobial)
points: Group A Streptococcus pyogenes or MRSA
May occur in young, immunocompetent patients
Associated with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
Rarely produces gas in soft tissues

steps.tx: To aid early bedside detection of necrotising soft tissue infections, clinicians utilize the **LRINEC score**, based on routine laboratory parameters. A score of six or higher raises strong suspicion of necrotising infection, while eight or above indicates high probability. Key laboratory variables include elevated C-reactive protein above one hundred and fifty milligrams per litre, leukocytosis, anaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperglycemia, and elevated serum creatinine reflecting acute end-organ hypoperfusion.
steps.say: Clinicians use the LRINEC score to identify necrotising fasciitis early. A score of six or higher raises suspicion, incorporating elevated C-reactive protein, leukocytosis, and hyponatraemia.

steps.tx: Immediate management of suspected necrotising fasciitis relies on aggressive physiological resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antimicrobials, and urgent, radical **surgical debridement**. Surgeons extend fascial incisions until healthy, adherent, bleeding tissue is encountered in all directions. Non-viable fascia separates effortlessly along the dishwater-fluid plane under finger dissection; patients require mandatory planned operative re-exploration within twenty-four hours to excise advancing necrosis.
steps.say: Suspected necrotising fasciitis mandates urgent radical surgical debridement. Surgeons resect all non-viable tissue until bleeding margins are reached, followed by planned re-exploration within twenty-four hours.

nodes.label: Early recognition: pain out of proportion and high LRINEC score
Aggressive crystalloids, blood cultures, and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Immediate emergency theatre: radical debridement of necrotic fascia
Planned second-look re-exploration in theatre at 24 to 48 hours
